titleStmt.title: Operant Conditioning of a Spinal Reflex Can Improve Locomotion after Spinal Cord Injury in Humans
titleStmt.author: Aiko K. Thompson
Ferne Pomerantz
Jonathan R. Wolpaw

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Operant Conditioning of a Spinal Reflex Can Improve Locomotion after Spinal Cord Injury in Humans

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The soleus H-reflex, and whether operantly down-conditioning it improves locomotion in people with chronic incomplete spinal cord injury.
span.quote: To explore the therapeutic application of these protocols, we studied the impact of down-conditioning the soleus H-reflex in people with impaired locomotion caused by chronic incomplete spinal cord injury.

span.label: Can people with chronic incomplete spinal cord injury down-condition the soleus H-reflex operantly, and if so is the reflex decrease accompanied by improved locomotion?
span.quote: This study asked two questions. First, can people with chronic SCI and impaired locomotion decrease the soleus H-reflex in response to an operant conditioning protocol? Second, if so, is H-reflex decrease associated with improved locomotion?

span.label: method
span.quote: They suggest that operant conditioning protocols could provide a valuable new approach to restoring useful function after spinal cord injuries or in other neuromuscular disorders.

span.label: operant down-conditioning of the soleus H-reflex
span.quote: To explore the therapeutic application of these protocols, we studied the impact of down-conditioning the soleus H-reflex in people with impaired locomotion caused by chronic incomplete spinal cord injury.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: After a baseline period in which soleus H-reflex size was measured and locomotion was assessed, subjects completed either 30 H-reflex down-conditioning sessions (DC subjects) or 30 sessions in which the H-reflex was simply measured [unconditioned (UC) subjects], and locomotion was reassessed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Acquiring the new smaller-reflex behaviour disturbs the post-injury spinal equilibrium and thereby triggers widespread adaptive plasticity that settles into a new equilibrium serving both the new reflex and locomotion
span.quote: It apparently triggered widespread adaptive plasticity that produced a new equilibrium that both decreased the H-reflex and improved locomotion.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In neurologically normal people, compensatory plasticity protecting already-satisfactory behaviours works against the long-term spinal change, which is why long-term change is smaller in them than in SCI subjects
span.quote: For behaviors such as locomotion, which are already satisfactory, these adaptations are likely to impede the long-term plasticity that decreases the H-reflex.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Injury to the corticospinal tract, the descending pathway that conditioning depends on, weakens the immediate cortical (task-dependent) component of the reflex change in SCI subjects
span.note: status: the paper's own words: may reflect
span.quote: The lesser task-dependent adaptation in subjects with SCI may reflect damage to the corticospinal tract (CST), the spinal cord pathway principally responsible for H-reflex conditioning

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Better bilateral modulation of ankle muscle activity yields more effective weight bearing and push-off, which in turn raises walking speed
span.quote: These bilateral improvements in the modulation of muscle activity controlling movement about the ankle joint probably resulted in more effective weight bearing and push off

span.label: Conditioned H-reflex change decomposes into a within-session task-dependent adaptation, read as cortical influence, plus an across-session long-term change, read as spinal cord plasticity
span.quote: Conditioned H-reflex change is composed of task-dependent adaptation (i.e., within-session difference between the control H-reflex and the conditioned H-reflex) plus long-term change (i.e., across-session change in the control H-reflex) ( Thompson et al., 2009 ).

span.label: The two components split differently after injury: less task-dependent adaptation, more long-term change, summing to the same total decrease as in normal subjects
span.quote: The greater decrease in the control H-reflex in the subjects with SCI combines with their lesser task-dependent adaptation to yield a decrease in the conditioned H-reflex that is identical to that found in normal subjects.

span.label: Reduced task-dependent adaptation after injury is attributed to damage to the corticospinal tract, on which reflex conditioning depends
span.quote: The lesser task-dependent adaptation in subjects with SCI may reflect damage to the corticospinal tract (CST), the spinal cord pathway principally responsible for H-reflex conditioning

span.label: In an uninjured cord, compensatory plasticity protects behaviours that are already satisfactory and thereby limits the long-term reflex change; after injury there is nothing to protect, so the change proceeds further
span.quote: For behaviors such as locomotion, which are already satisfactory, these adaptations are likely to impede the long-term plasticity that decreases the H-reflex.

span.label: Acquiring the new reflex disturbs the equilibrium the injured cord had settled into, triggering wider plasticity that changes locomotion as a whole rather than one pathway
span.quote: It apparently triggered widespread adaptive plasticity that produced a new equilibrium that both decreased the H-reflex and improved locomotion.

span.label: After injury the long-term change is doubly rewarded - it satisfies the conditioning criterion and it improves walking - which is offered as why it goes further than in normal subjects
span.quote: In these SCI rats, as in the subjects of this study, the long-term change in the H-reflex is doubly adaptive: it increases reward probability in the conditioning protocol, and it also improves locomotion.

span.label: The success rate, though not significantly below that of normal subjects, was lower, and applicability to more severe impairment is unknown.
span.note: what this limits: the transfer of the method to more impaired patients: THEIR SUCCESS RATE WAS NOT SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENT FROM THAT OF NORMAL SUBJECTS ... IT WAS LOWER
span.quote: Although their success rate was not significantly different from that of normal subjects ( Thompson et al., 2009 ), it was lower; and the extent to which reflex conditioning is possible in people with more severe impairments is unclear.

span.label: The small H-reflex increase seen in the unconditioned control group may be a nonspecific effect of repeated exposure to the measurement protocol.
span.note: what this limits: the control-group baseline drift: THIS MAY HAVE BEEN A NONSPECIFIC EFFECT OF CONTINUED EXPOSURE OVER 30 SESSIONS TO THE BASELINE PROTOCOL
span.quote: This may have been a nonspecific effect of continued exposure over 30 sessions to the baseline protocol of standing, providing soleus background EMG, and having the H-reflex elicited.

span.label: Thirteen subjects, of whom only six showed the effect, and the comparison group has four
span.note: what this limits: every group-level statistic: 13 AMBULATORY SUBJECTS, of whom only six showed the effect, against a comparison group of four
span.quote: The study participants were 13 ambulatory subjects (9 men and 4 women; age range, 28–68 years; mean ± SD age, 48.4 ± 13.9 years)

span.label: All subjects were AIS grade C or D, so the protocol is untested in more severe injury and requires surviving supraspinal input
span.note: what this limits: any extension to more severe injury: THE NEED FOR SUPRASPINAL INPUT WILL REMAIN, and all subjects here retained it
span.quote: While future improvements in the conditioning protocol may increase success, the need for supraspinal input will remain.

span.label: The subjects who improved are the same subjects in whom conditioning worked, so improvement and successful conditioning cannot be separated from subject-level differences
span.note: what this limits: the walking-improvement result, which is not independent of the conditioning result: THE IMPROVEMENT ... DID NOT OCCUR IN PEOPLE IN WHOM THE H-REFLEX DID NOT DECREASE, WHETHER THEY WERE UC SUBJECTS OR UNSUCCESSFUL DC SUBJECTS
span.quote: The improvement was evident both in quantitative testing and, most important, to the subjects themselves in their daily lives. It did not occur in people in whom the H-reflex did not decrease, whether they were UC subjects or unsuccessful DC subjects.

span.label: The breadth of the effect exceeds what the manipulated pathway can explain, and the wider plasticity invoked to cover the gap is inferred rather than measured
span.note: what this limits: the proposed mechanism's sufficiency: IT IS UNLIKELY THAT THE PLASTICITY UNDERLYING A SMALLER SOLEUS H-REFLEX IN ONE LEG COULD ITSELF HAVE SUCH BROAD BENEFICIAL EFFECTS ON WALKING
span.quote: It is unlikely that the plasticity underlying a smaller soleus H-reflex in one leg could itself have such broad beneficial effects on walking, including increasing the locomotor EMG modulation of contralateral muscles.

span.label: The normal-subject comparison values are drawn from an earlier study rather than a concurrent control group
span.note: what this limits: every comparison against normal values: THE DATA FOR NORMAL DC SUBJECTS ARE FROM THOMPSON ET AL. (2009), not from a concurrent control group
span.quote: The data for normal DC subjects are from Thompson et al. (2009) .

span.label: The subject comments are unsolicited and unblinded, and the subjects knew which protocol they were on
span.note: what this limits: the subjects' own reports of benefit: OVER THE 3 MONTHS OF THE STUDY, THE SUBJECTS WERE NOT ASKED ABOUT THE CURRENT STATE OF THEIR MOTOR FUNCTION - unsolicited and unblinded
span.quote: Over the 3 months of the study, the subjects were not asked about the current state of their motor function or whether their disabilities had changed in any way.

span.label: The comparison group's reflex drifted upward over the same period, which the authors attribute to nonspecific exposure rather than measure
span.note: duplicate of: limitations[1] · what this limits: the same scope as item 1 - the control group's reflex drifted upward over the same period, attributed to nonspecific exposure to the baseline procedure rather than to conditioning
span.quote: This may have been a nonspecific effect of continued exposure over 30 sessions to the baseline protocol of standing, providing soleus background EMG, and having the H-reflex elicited.

span.label: control trials in which the visual feedback shows only background EMG and nothing about H-reflex size - the weakest entry in this sample, carried by the word SIMPLY
span.note: eliminates: prestimulus background EMG differing between control and conditioning trials, so a change in the reflex cannot be a posture or muscle-activation effect
span.quote: Thus, for each control trial, the visual feedback simply helped the subject maintain the required prestimulus background EMG activity.

span.label: H-reflex - conditioned: the average over the 225 feedback trials, the reflex the subject was actively trying to change
span.quote: This value is called the conditioned H-reflex size (regardless of whether the session is from a DC subject or a UC subject).

span.label: H-reflex - control: the average over 20 trials with no feedback and no instruction, which is what shows whether the change persists when the subject is not trying
span.quote: In addition, for each session of each subject we determined the average H-reflex size for 20 control trials. This value is called the control H-reflex size.

span.label: H-reflex - locomotor: the average across 12 step-cycle bins during walking, a different behavioural context from the standing measurement
span.quote: As described above for locomotor EMG analysis, the step cycle was divided into 12 bins of equal duration, and average H-reflex size for each bin was determined. The average of these 12 values defined the average locomotor H-reflex.

span.label: H-reflex - maximum (H max): the peak of the recruitment curve, a property of the pathway rather than of a trial
span.quote: Stimulus intensity was varied in increments of 1.25–2.50 mA from below soleus H-reflex threshold, to the maximum H-reflex (H max ), to an intensity just above that needed to elicit the maximum M-wave (M max )

span.label: success - within a trial: the reflex fell below the current criterion value, shown to the subject as a green bar
span.quote: The bar was green (indicating success) when the H-reflex fell within the shaded area (i.e., was below the criterion value), and the bar was red (indicating failure) when the H-reflex size was not below the criterion value.

span.label: success - across the study: the last six conditioning sessions differed significantly from baseline, which is the sense in which two-thirds of subjects succeeded
span.quote: The filled triangles represent the DC subjects in whom down-conditioning was successful (i.e., the average conditioned H-reflexes for conditioning sessions 25–30 were significantly less than those for the 6 baseline sessions).

span.label: modulation - of EMG across the step cycle: how much a muscle varies its own activity, captured by the modulation index
span.quote: The degree to which each muscle's activity was modulated during locomotion was determined by calculating its modulation index (MI) in percent as: 100 × [(highest bin amplitude − lowest bin amplitude)/highest bin amplitude]

span.label: modulation - of the reflex across the step cycle: how reflex size varies by phase, which should be lowest in swing and becomes so after conditioning
span.quote: In addition, its modulation across the step cycle has become more normal: the reflex is smallest during the swing phase.

span.label: change - task-dependent adaptation: the within-session difference between control and conditioned reflex, produced immediately on being asked
span.quote: This difference represents task-dependent adaptation; that is, the decrease that the subjects were able to produce immediately when they were asked to decrease the H-reflex.

span.label: claim_type: method
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: method — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: These results indicate that reflex-conditioning protocols might help to restore motor function after SCI or in other disorders.

span.label: method: behavioural-experiment
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: behavioural-experiment — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: The subjects were randomly assigned (at a 2:1 ratio) to the down-conditioning (DC) group

span.label: phenomenon: operant down-conditioning of the soleus H-reflex
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: operant down-conditioning of the soleus H-reflex — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Operant conditioning protocols can modify the activity of specific spinal cord pathways and can thereby affect behaviors that use these pathways.

span.label: builds-on → Thompson et al. (2009) human soleus H-reflex conditioning protocol in neurologically normal subjects
span.quote: The operant conditioning protocol for the human soleus H-reflex was originally developed in a study of neurologically normal subjects and is described in detail in Thompson et al. (2009)

span.label: extends → Chen et al. (2006b) soleus H-reflex conditioning in spinal cord-injured rats
span.quote: In rats in which a lateralized spinal cord injury (SCI) had produced a gait asymmetry, appropriate conditioning of the soleus H-reflex on the injured side eliminated the asymmetry and restored more normal locomotion ( Chen et al., 2006b ).

span.label: replicates → Chen et al. (2006b) and Segal and Wolf (1994)
span.quote: This finding is consistent with results for soleus H-reflex conditioning in spinal cord-injured rats ( Chen et al., 2006b ) and biceps spinal stretch reflex conditioning in people with SCI ( Segal and Wolf, 1994 ).

span.label: extends → Thompson et al. 2009, the same conditioning protocol in neurologically normal subjects
span.quote: The operant conditioning protocol for the human soleus H-reflex was originally developed in a study of neurologically normal subjects and is described in detail in Thompson et al. (2009) .

span.label: extends → Chen et al. 2006b, H-reflex conditioning in spinal cord-injured rats
span.quote: In rats in which a lateralized spinal cord injury (SCI) had produced a gait asymmetry, appropriate conditioning of the soleus H-reflex on the injured side eliminated the asymmetry and restored more normal locomotion ( Chen et al., 2006b ).

span.label: supports → Wolpaw 2010, the negotiated equilibrium hypothesis
span.quote: Wolpaw (2010) hypothesizes that spinal neurons and pathways are maintained in a state of “negotiated equilibrium,” a balance that ensures the satisfactory performance of all the behaviors in the individual's current repertoire ( Nielsen et al., 1993 ; Ozmerdivenli et al., 2002 ; Zehr, 2006 ).

span.label: supports → Segal and Wolf 1994, spinal stretch reflex conditioning in people with SCI
span.quote: This finding is consistent with results for soleus H-reflex conditioning in spinal cord-injured rats ( Chen et al., 2006b ) and biceps spinal stretch reflex conditioning in people with SCI ( Segal and Wolf, 1994 ).

span.label: task-dependent adaptation —part-of→ H-reflex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Conditioned H-reflex change is composed of task-dependent adaptation (i.e., within-session difference between the control H-reflex and the conditioned H-reflex) plus long-term change (i.e., across-session change in the control H-reflex) ( Thompson et al., 2009 ).

span.label: long-term change —part-of→ H-reflex
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Conditioned H-reflex change is composed of task-dependent adaptation (i.e., within-session difference between the control H-reflex and the conditioned H-reflex) plus long-term change (i.e., across-session change in the control H-reflex) ( Thompson et al., 2009 ).

span.label: task-dependent adaptation —contrasted-with→ long-term change
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Task-dependent adaptation was significantly less in subjects with SCI than in neurologically normal subjects (−7% vs −15%), while long-term change was significantly more (−24% vs −16%).

span.label: long-term change —operationalised-as→ spinal cord plasticity
span.note: status: AN ATTRIBUTED INTERPRETATION, AND THE TWO HALVES OF THE SENTENCE ARE NOT EQUALLY HEDGED: 'The former IS THOUGHT TO reflect immediate change in cortical influence (e.g., on presynaptic inhibition), WHILE THE LATTER REFLECTS spinal cord plasticity.' The first clause reports what the field holds and the second asserts plainly - the same sentence carries an attributed belief and a direct claim, and this edge is cut from across both. · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: In neurologically normal subjects, the spinal cord plasticity responsible for the long-term change in the H-reflex is likely to disturb behaviors such as locomotion, which are already satisfactory; and it may thereby lead to additional plasticity that compensates for the change in the H-reflex pathway.

span.label: modulation index —operationalised-as→ step cycle
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: For analysis of locomotor EMG activity, the complete step cycle was divided into 12 bins of equal duration ( Kido et al., 2004a ; Makihara et al., 2012 ).

span.label: step-cycle symmetry —operationalised-as→ step cycle
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: To assess gait quality, we examined step-cycle symmetry (i.e., the ratio of the time between the nFC and the cFC to the time between cFC and nFC). A ratio of 1 indicates a symmetrical gait. Spontaneous

span.label: spasticity —causes→ swing phase
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: During the baseline period, the ratio was always >1 because foot drop and/or spasticity prolonged the swing phase of the conditioned leg (which was the more impaired leg) and/or because spasticity and the resulting instability in the conditioned leg shortened its stance (i.e., weight-bearing) phase.

span.label: hyperreflexia —causes→ locomotion
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The present study down-conditioned the soleus H-reflex because locomotion was impaired by hyperreflexia.

span.label: down-conditioning —causes→ spinal cord plasticity
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: It apparently triggered widespread adaptive plasticity that produced a new equilibrium that both decreased the H-reflex and improved locomotion.

span.label: corticospinal tract —causes→ task-dependent adaptation
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak
span.quote: The lesser task-dependent adaptation in subjects with SCI may reflect damage to the corticospinal tract (CST), the spinal cord pathway principally responsible for H-reflex conditioning

span.label: down-conditioning —distinct-from→ up-conditioning
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: In contrast, the study by Chen et al. (2006b) in spinal cord-injured rats up-conditioned the soleus H-reflex because locomotion was impaired by weak right stance.

span.label: soleus —contrasted-with→ tibialis anterior
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: EMG activity from soleus and its antagonist tibialis anterior (TA) was recorded with surface self-adhesive Ag-AgCl electrodes (2.2 × 3.5 cm, Vermed), amplified, bandpass filtered (10–1000 Hz), digitized (5000 Hz), and stored.

span.label: operant conditioning —contrasted-with→ negotiated equilibrium
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: In normal subjects, the spinal cord plasticity underlying the new behavior (i.e., a smaller H-reflex) requires the creation of a new equilibrium that produces a smaller H-reflex and still continues to serve other behaviors satisfactorily.

span.label: down-conditioning —contrasted-with→ Modified Ashworth scale
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7
span.quote: This flexibility and specificity are distinctive and desirable features of this new therapeutic approach; and they distinguish it from less focused interventions such as botulinum toxin or baclofen, which simply weaken muscles or reflexes and may have undesirable side effects

span.label: H-reflex —contrasted-with→ M-wave
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: At each intensity, four EMG responses were averaged to measure the H-reflex and M-wave.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: were compared with the average H-reflexes for the 225 trials of the three 75-trial blocks of the six baseline sessions by unpaired t test (two tailed)

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The increase was substantial and significant in the six DC subjects in whom the H-reflex decreased [(mean ± SE) +59 ± 19%; p = 0.03, paired t test].

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: a repeated-measures ANOVA was applied to the mean values across successive six-session blocks beginning with the six baseline sessions

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: and only 5 positive comments by the other seven subjects ( p = 0.0027, Mann–Whitney U test)

span.label: p-value
span.quote: and only 5 positive comments by the other seven subjects ( p = 0.0027, Mann–Whitney U test)

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: The study participants were 13 ambulatory subjects (9 men and 4 women; age range, 28–68 years; mean ± SD age, 48.4 ± 13.9 years)

span.label: standard error
span.quote: At both 1 month and 3 months, the conditioned H-reflex remained reduced in every subject, averaging (mean ± SE) 65 ± 10% and 58 ± 10% of baseline values, respectively.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: and the DC and UC groups differed significantly in final H-reflex size ( p = 0.025 by unpaired t test).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Second, the final value of the control H-reflex in the subjects with SCI is significantly smaller than in normal subjects (i.e., 76 ± 9% of baseline vs 84 ± 6%, respectively; p = 0.01, two-tailed t test).

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: 25 of the 30 positive comments were made by the six DC subjects in whom down-conditioning was successful, and only 5 positive comments by the other seven subjects ( p = 0.0027, Mann–Whitney U test).

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: The DC and UC groups did not differ significantly in soleus and TA background EMG levels ( p = 0.90 and 0.81 by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, respectively), M-wave sizes ( p = 0.71), or baseline H-reflex sizes ( p = 0.11).

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: To assess the stability of soleus M max , soleus M-wave size in control and conditioning trials, and soleus and TA background EMG levels, a repeated-measures ANOVA was applied to the mean values across successive six-session blocks beginning with the six baseline sessions.

span.label: standard error
span.quote: averaging (mean ± SE) 65 ± 10% and 58 ± 10% of baseline values, respectively

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: age range, 28–68 years; mean ± SD age, 48.4 ± 13.9 years

span.label: p-value
span.quote: In the DC subjects in whom the H-reflex decreased, the average MI rose significantly [from (mean ± SD) 74 ±17% to 80 ± 11%; p = 0.005, paired t test].

span.label: p-value
span.quote: In the successful DC subjects, the H max measured at the beginning of each session also decreased with down-conditioning, paralleling the changes in the control H-reflex [final value (mean ± SE), 84 ± 5% of baseline; p < 0.001, paired t test].

span.label: Six of the nine people with spinal cord injury successfully down-conditioned the soleus H-reflex, a 67% success rate not significantly below the 89% seen in neurologically normal subjects.
span.quote: The success rate for the subjects with SCI (i.e., 6/9 or 67%) is slightly, but not significantly, less than that for neurologically normal subjects (i.e., 8/9 or 89%)

span.label: The H-reflex decrease was specific to the conditioning protocol: no unconditioned subject's reflex fell, and the two groups' final reflex sizes differed significantly.
span.quote: In contrast, the conditioned H-reflex did not decrease significantly in any of the UC subjects; and the DC and UC groups differed significantly in final H-reflex size

span.label: Ten-metre walking speed rose by an average of 59% in the six subjects whose H-reflex decreased.
span.quote: The increase was substantial and significant in the six DC subjects in whom the H-reflex decreased [(mean ± SE) +59 ± 19%; p = 0.03, paired t test].

span.label: Gait symmetry moved toward the ideal ratio of 1 in every subject whose H-reflex decreased.
span.quote: After the 30 conditioning or control sessions, this ratio decreased in every subject in whom the H-reflex decreased, becoming closer to 1

span.label: In subjects whose H-reflex did not decrease, gait actually became less symmetrical over the same 30 sessions.
span.quote: In contrast, the ratio increased in every subject in whom the H-reflex did not decrease

span.label: Successful down-conditioning of one leg's soleus reflex increased step-cycle EMG modulation in ankle and knee flexors and extensors of both legs, not just the conditioned leg.
span.quote: Thus, successful H-reflex down-conditioning was associated with a significant increase in the degree to which ankle and knee flexor and extensor muscles of both legs modulated their activity in synchrony with the step cycle.

span.label: Although the total reflex decrease matched that of normal subjects, its composition differed: SCI subjects showed less immediate task-dependent adaptation (-7% vs -15%) and more long-term across-session change (-24% vs -16%).
span.quote: Task-dependent adaptation was significantly less in subjects with SCI than in neurologically normal subjects (−7% vs −15%), while long-term change was significantly more (−24% vs −16%).

span.label: Unprompted positive reports of improved walking clustered almost entirely in the six successfully conditioned subjects (25 of 30 comments).
span.quote: The contrast is striking: 25 of the 30 positive comments were made by the six DC subjects in whom down-conditioning was successful, and only 5 positive comments by the other seven subjects

span.label: The reflex decrease persisted after training stopped, averaging 65% of baseline at one month and 58% at three months.
span.quote: At both 1 month and 3 months, the conditioned H-reflex remained reduced in every subject, averaging (mean ± SE) 65 ± 10% and 58 ± 10% of baseline values, respectively.

span.label: The reflex reduction carried over into walking itself: the H-reflex elicited during locomotion fell to 59% of its baseline size.
span.quote: In the successful DC subjects, the average locomotor H-reflex also decreased [to (mean ± SE) 59 ± 17% of baseline value; p = 0.04 by paired t test].

span.label: the conditioned H-reflex fell to the same 69% of baseline in SCI subjects as in normal subjects, but by a different mix of components
span.quote: First, the final average value of the conditioned H-reflex (i.e., the average of the last three conditioning sessions) in the subjects with SCI is identical to that in normal subjects [i.e., (mean ± SE) 69 ± 11% and 69 ± 6% of baseline, respectively].

span.label: task-dependent adaptation was smaller and long-term change larger after injury
span.quote: Task-dependent adaptation is greater in the normal subjects, while change in the control H-reflex is greater in the subjects with SCI.

span.label: reflex decrease was specific to the down-conditioning protocol and absent in the unconditioned group
span.quote: Thus, H-reflex decrease was specific to the DC group.

span.label: the unconditioned group's reflex rose slightly but significantly over the same period
span.quote: Indeed, it should be noted that the UC group as a whole showed a slight but significant increase in the conditioned H-reflex [to (mean ± SE) 116 ± 7% of baseline; p = 0.05 by paired t test].

span.label: walking speed rose 59% on average in subjects whose reflex decreased and not significantly in those whose did not
span.quote: The increase was substantial and significant in the six DC subjects in whom the H-reflex decreased [(mean ± SE) +59 ± 19%; p = 0.03, paired t test].

span.label: gait symmetry improved in every subject whose reflex decreased and worsened in every subject whose did not
span.quote: After the 30 conditioning or control sessions, this ratio decreased in every subject in whom the H-reflex decreased, becoming closer to 1 ( p = 0.05, paired t test). In contrast, the ratio increased in every subject in whom the H-reflex did not decrease ( p = 0.02).

span.label: EMG modulation improved bilaterally, not only in the conditioned leg
span.quote: This improvement was bilateral; it was not limited to the muscles of the conditioned leg.

span.label: the reflex decrease persisted at one, three and in one case six months
span.quote: At both 1 month and 3 months, the conditioned H-reflex remained reduced in every subject, averaging (mean ± SE) 65 ± 10% and 58 ± 10% of baseline values, respectively.

span.label: unsolicited positive comments clustered in the successful group and only after the reflex had substantially decreased
span.quote: Furthermore, and most importantly, these comments did not occur until the decrease in the conditioned H-reflex was substantial and the decrease in the control reflex had begun (i.e., the 12th conditioning session and later; Fig. 3 ).

span.label: two subjects reduced their reliance on a walking aid
span.quote: Furthermore, the two subjects who increased their walking speeds most also decreased their dependence on an assistive device in their daily lives: one switched from a walker to crutches, and the other switched from a walker to a cane.

span.label: the success rate in SCI subjects was 67%, not significantly below the 89% seen in normal subjects
span.quote: The success rate for the subjects with SCI (i.e., 6/9 or 67%) is slightly, but not significantly, less than that for neurologically normal subjects (i.e., 8/9 or 89%) ( Thompson et al., 2009 ) or for normal monkeys, rats, and mice (i.e., 75–80%) ( Wolpaw et al., 1983 ; Wolpaw, 1987 ; Chen and Wolpaw, 1995 ; Carp et al., 2006b ).

span.label: stimulus and recording conditions were stable across all sessions, ruling out measurement drift as the source of the reflex change
span.quote: Soleus M max , soleus M-wave size during H-reflex elicitation, and soleus and TA background EMG levels remained stable across all the sessions in both the DC and UC groups ( p > 0.33 for all of these measures in both groups, one-way repeated-measures ANOVA).

span.label: H-reflex size
span.quote: H-reflex size was defined as the average absolute value of soleus EMG (i.e., equivalent to rectified EMG) in the H-reflex interval (typically 30–45 ms after the stimulus) minus the average absolute value of soleus background EMG.

span.label: conditioned H-reflex size
